description: Team A applies an RBF kernel SVM to a text classification problem with 50,000 TF-IDF features (document-term frequencies). The training takes 18 hours with poor performance. Team B applies a linear SVM to the same data and achieves good performance in 20 minutes. Why does the RBF kernel hurt here when it helps with concentric-circle problems?
options: RBF kernel SVMs cannot process sparse data like TF-IDF features — they require dense, continuous feature vectors to function correctly

In high-dimensional spaces, points are already approximately equidistant from each other, making the RBF similarity function near-zero for almost all pairs and destroying its ability to separate classes
Linear SVMs are always faster than kernel SVMs regardless of data type, so the RBF kernel is never the right choice for large-scale problems
TF-IDF features have values between 0 and 1, and RBF kernels require features on a larger scale to compute meaningful distances
explanation:
The curse of dimensionality strikes RBF kernels in high-dimensional spaces. The RBF kernel K(x, y) = exp(-γ||x-y||²) depends on pairwise Euclidean distances. In 50,000 dimensions, due to the concentration of measure phenomenon, all pairs of points tend toward the same average distance — points cluster near a hypersphere shell rather than dispersing. The exponential of a large, nearly-constant distance makes the kernel value near-zero for almost all pairs, collapsing the kernel matrix to near-identical values and destroying the discriminative structure.

Text data in high-dimensional TF-IDF space is already 'spread out' — the problem is inherently nearly-linearly separable in this high-dimensional space (sparse, binary-like features with clear class-word associations). A linear SVM is sufficient and appropriate.

RBF kernels are designed to map low-dimensional data to a higher-dimensional space for better separability. When the data is already in very high dimensions, this mapping is redundant and the distance-based similarity function degrades.

Option A is wrong: RBF kernels can technically be applied to sparse data, though they are rarely appropriate. The problem is the high dimensionality, not the sparsity.

Option C is wrong: for low-dimensional, non-linearly-separable data (like the concentric circles), RBF kernels are appropriate. It is specifically high-dimensional data where linear SVMs are typically preferred.

Option D is wrong: the scale of TF-IDF features is not the issue. Even with normalised features, high-dimensional distance concentration occurs.
hints: The RBF kernel measures similarity as a function of distance. What happens to the distribution of pairwise distances in 50,000 dimensions — do they concentrate or spread out?
If the kernel matrix K(x, y) has nearly identical values for all pairs (x, y), what can the SVM learn from it? What discriminative information is available?

title: Clustering Evaluation: Elbow Method Limitations
description: You apply k-means to a dataset and plot within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS/inertia) for k=1 through k=15. The curve decreases steeply from k=1 to k=5, then continues decreasing gradually but never shows a clear 'elbow'. A colleague says 'with no clear elbow, we cannot determine the right k.' Is this correct?
options: Yes — the elbow method is the gold standard for k selection and if no elbow appears, k-means is not appropriate for this dataset

Partially — the elbow method often fails to produce a clear elbow, particularly when true clusters are not well-separated. Complementary methods like silhouette scores or domain knowledge should be used
No — the correct k is always the one that minimises WCSS, which is k equal to the number of data points (every point is its own cluster)
No — the absence of an elbow means k=2 is always the correct choice because the first split accounts for the largest drop in WCSS
explanation:
The elbow method frequently fails to produce a clear elbow in practice. The method works best when clusters are well-separated with low within-cluster variance — a scenario where adding a new cluster produces a dramatic jump in improvement, followed by diminishing returns. But real-world data often has gradual cluster structure with overlapping groups, producing a smooth curve without a clear elbow.

When the elbow method is ambiguous, complementary approaches include: silhouette analysis (measures how similar each point is to its own cluster vs other clusters), gap statistic (compares WCSS to a null reference distribution), domain knowledge (the business might know how many segments make operational sense), or hierarchical clustering dendrograms (can reveal natural cut points).

Option A is wrong: the absence of a clear elbow does not mean k-means is inappropriate — it means the elbow method is not informative for this dataset. k-means may still produce useful segments.

Option C is wrong: minimising WCSS unconditionally gives k = number of data points, which is trivially useless. The elbow method specifically looks for a point of diminishing returns.

Option D is wrong: k=2 is not a default when no elbow appears. The first split always produces the largest WCSS drop because going from 1 to 2 clusters is the biggest structural change. This does not mean 2 is the right number of clusters.
hints: The elbow method looks for a 'kink' in the WCSS curve. Why might real-world data, with gradually overlapping clusters, produce a smooth curve instead of a sharp kink?
What are you actually trying to measure when selecting k? WCSS is one proxy, but it always decreases with k. What other signals can help you determine the right number of clusters?

title: Clustering Evaluation: Silhouette Score Interpretation
description: After running k-means with k=4, you compute silhouette scores for each data point. You find: Cluster 1 has average silhouette score 0.72, Cluster 2 has 0.68, Cluster 3 has 0.41, Cluster 4 has -0.12. The overall average silhouette is 0.44. What do these scores indicate about the clustering quality?
options: The clustering is high quality — an overall score of 0.44 exceeds the typical threshold of 0.25 for a valid clustering

Clusters 1 and 2 are well-separated and internally compact, Cluster 3 is questionable with points on the boundary between clusters, and Cluster 4 is likely misclustered — its points may belong to a different cluster
The silhouette score only measures internal compactness, not separation — to evaluate separation, you need to use WCSS, which is a different metric
All four clusters are good — silhouette scores above 0 are always acceptable, and -0.12 indicates only a slight boundary effect in Cluster 4
explanation:
Silhouette score for a point is (b - a) / max(a, b), where a = average distance to points in the same cluster (cohesion) and b = average distance to points in the nearest other cluster (separation). The score ranges from -1 to 1.

Score close to 1: the point is well inside its cluster and far from others. Score near 0: the point is on the boundary between two clusters. Negative score: the point is closer to a different cluster than its own assigned cluster — it is likely misassigned.

Cluster 4 with average -0.12 means many of its points are closer to another cluster than to their own — these points are probably misclustered. This is a significant problem: Cluster 4 may not be a genuine cluster, or k=4 may have one too many clusters, causing k-means to split a natural cluster into two pieces and create an artificial fourth cluster.

Option A is wrong: the 0.44 average obscures the serious problem in Cluster 4. Averaging a strong cluster with a bad one does not make the bad one acceptable.

Option C is wrong: silhouette score directly incorporates both internal cohesion (a) and separation from nearest other cluster (b). It measures both simultaneously.

Option D is wrong: a negative silhouette score is not a 'slight boundary effect'. It means the point is, on average, closer to a different cluster — indicating systematic misassignment, not a borderline case.
hints: The silhouette score compares a point's distance to its own cluster (a) vs the nearest other cluster (b). What does it mean when b < a, i.e., a point is closer to a different cluster than its own?
Look at Cluster 4 in isolation: if the average score is negative, how many points within that cluster are likely closer to another cluster? Is this a well-defined cluster?

title: Cross-Validation: Time-Series Split
description: You are evaluating a model that predicts next-week sales based on 3 years of weekly data (156 weeks). You apply standard 5-fold cross-validation, randomly shuffling weeks across folds. A colleague argues you should use time-series cross-validation (walk-forward validation) instead. Beyond the data leakage concern, what is a second practical reason to prefer time-series CV for this problem?
options: Time-series CV uses more data for training since each fold is larger than a random fold of the same size
Random shuffling breaks temporal autocorrelation, so the model trained on shuffled data may not learn the dynamics relevant to the deployment scenario where it always predicts the next period
Time-series CV prevents the model from seeing the same week in both training and validation, which standard k-fold allows
Random k-fold is invalid for sales data because sales values are always positive, and cross-validation requires normally distributed target values
explanation:
The second concern beyond data leakage is distributional mismatch. In deployment, the model always uses historical data to predict the next period — the temporal direction is fixed. With random shuffling, the model trains on arbitrary mixtures of past and future data, learning statistical relationships that may not reflect the true temporal dynamics.

In time-series data, patterns like trend, seasonality, and autocorrelation are direction-dependent. A model trained on randomly shuffled weeks learns 'static' feature-target associations but does not learn to predict forward in time. The evaluation on randomly shuffled validation folds measures whether the model can interpolate between known time periods — not whether it can extrapolate to future periods. In deployment, it must extrapolate.

Walk-forward validation trains on all data up to time t and evaluates on t+1, simulating the exact deployment scenario. Each fold represents 'predict the future given the past'.

Option A is wrong: time-series CV typically uses less data for early folds (just the first few periods) and more for later folds. It does not consistently use more data than random k-fold.

Option C is wrong: standard k-fold does ensure each data point appears in exactly one validation fold and the remaining k-1 folds for training. The same week does not appear in both training and validation within the same fold.

Option D is wrong: there is no requirement for normally distributed targets in cross-validation. This is a misconception.
hints: In deployment, the model always predicts the future given the past — it never predicts the past given the future. Does random shuffling preserve this directionality?

Think about what the model learns when trained on shuffled time series: it learns feature-target relationships without regard to temporal order. Does the evaluation on shuffled validation data measure whether the model can predict forward in time?

title: Cross-Validation: Group K-Fold for Patient Data
description: A healthcare model predicts patient readmission risk. The dataset has 50,000 rows representing individual hospital visits, but only 8,000 unique patients — many patients have multiple visits. A data scientist applies standard 5-fold cross-validation at the visit level (each row is assigned to a fold randomly). A senior ML engineer flags this as a serious problem. Why?
options: 5-fold cross-validation is too few folds for a dataset with only 8,000 unique patients — at least 10 folds are needed for stable estimates

Random visit-level splitting allows the same patient's data to appear in both training and validation folds. The model learns patient-specific patterns and its performance on validation visits from known patients overestimates true generalisation to new patients
Healthcare data requires stratified cross-validation to ensure equal readmission rates across folds — the issue is class balance, not patient overlap
The problem is that 50,000 rows is too large for cross-validation — a simple holdout split is more computationally appropriate at this scale
explanation:
This is the group leakage problem. When multiple rows belong to the same patient and those rows are randomly split across folds, visits from the same patient appear in both training and validation. The model learns patient-specific features (stable factors like age, chronic conditions, insurance type) from the patient's training visits and then 'predicts' those same features on the validation visits — producing unrealistically high performance.

In deployment, the model will encounter new patients it has never seen. Its true generalisation ability is whether it can predict readmission for a patient it has no historical data on — not whether it can predict the next visit for a patient it was trained on.

The correct approach is group k-fold cross-validation: assign all visits for a given patient to the same fold. Each fold then contains completely held-out patients, not held-out visits from known patients. This correctly simulates deployment performance.

Option A is wrong: the number of folds is a secondary concern. The fundamental structural problem is patient leakage across folds.

Option C is wrong: stratification for class balance is a real consideration but is not the 'serious problem' the engineer is flagging. The primary issue is that the model trains and validates on the same patients.

Option D is wrong: 50,000 rows is not too large for cross-validation. Cross-validation is scale-agnostic; the choice between CV and holdout is not driven by dataset size.
hints: If Patient A has 6 visits and those visits are randomly split across 5 folds, how many folds will have some of Patient A's visits in training? What does the model learn about Patient A that helps it on Patient A's validation visits?
The question to ask is: what does 'generalisation' mean for this model in deployment — generalising to new visits from known patients, or generalising to entirely new patients it has never seen?

title: Ensemble Depth: Why More Trees Don't Overfit in Random Forests
description: A random forest consistently improves validation performance as you add trees from 10 to 500, plateauing around 300. A gradient boosted model, by contrast, improves with more trees until around 150, then degrades. Why does adding trees not cause overfitting in random forests but does in gradient boosting?
options: Random forests are trained with cross-validation internally, preventing individual trees from overfitting; gradient boosting is not

Random forest trees are independent and averaged — adding more independent averaged predictions reduces variance monotonically without increasing bias; gradient boosted trees are sequential and each new tree introduces a small bias correction that accumulates into overfitting if continued too long
Random forests use deeper trees that are individually more accurate, so adding more improves performance without variance risk
Gradient boosting overfits because it uses the entire training set for each tree, while random forests use bootstrap samples that prevent any single pattern from dominating
explanation:
The key difference is the nature of averaging in random forests vs sequential fitting in gradient boosting.

Random forest: each tree is trained independently on a bootstrap sample. Adding more trees is equivalent to taking a larger average of independent, identically distributed estimates. By the law of large numbers, a larger average has lower variance. Crucially, adding more trees does not change the expected value (bias) of the estimate — only its variance. So the ensemble improves monotonically (lower variance) until it plateaus at the irreducible variance floor.

Gradient boosting: each tree is a correction to the previous ensemble's residuals. With a fixed learning rate, adding more trees continues to correct smaller and smaller residuals — eventually fitting the noise in the residuals. This is genuine overfitting: the new trees are learning the specific noise of the training set rather than generalisable patterns.

Option A is wrong: random forests are not trained with internal cross-validation. Individual trees are allowed to overfit their bootstrap samples — it is the averaging that reduces overall variance.

Option C is wrong: random forests typically use shallower trees than fully grown unpruned trees, and depth is not the reason adding trees helps.

Option D is wrong: gradient boosting also typically uses subsampling (stochastic gradient boosting), which partially addresses this. The fundamental difference is sequential vs independent fitting, not bootstrap sampling.
hints: Consider the statistical property of averaging independent estimates: what happens to variance as you take the average of more and more independent random variables? Does the expected value (bias) change?
In gradient boosting, each tree is not independent — it depends on the residuals of the previous ensemble. What happens when the residuals get very small and the remaining signal is mostly noise?

title: Class Imbalance and Threshold Selection for Business Objectives
description: A subscription service builds a churn prediction model. The model outputs probabilities and at threshold=0.5 achieves: precision=0.55, recall=0.40, F1=0.47. The retention team can reach out to at most 500 customers per week (capacity constraint). The total customer base is 20,000. A team lead asks: 'We need to maximise the number of churners we actually retain — how should we set the threshold?' What is the correct approach?
options: Lower the threshold to 0.1 to maximise recall — catching more churners at any precision is always better than missing them
Keep threshold at 0.5 — this is the mathematically correct threshold for balanced precision-recall and changing it would be arbitrary
Set the threshold to flag the top 500 highest-probability customers, not based on a fixed probability cutoff, since the constraint is a fixed capacity, not a probability threshold
Raise the threshold to improve precision — the retention team should only contact customers the model is highly confident about
explanation:
When there is a fixed capacity constraint (top-N customers, not a probability threshold), the correct framing is rank-based, not threshold-based. The team should take the 500 customers with the highest predicted churn probability — regardless of what probability value that corresponds to.

A fixed threshold (e.g. 0.5, 0.3, or 0.1) might return 200 customers (too few, leaving capacity unused) or 3,000 customers (too many, requiring triaging). The capacity-constrained problem is: 'given I can act on exactly 500, which 500 should I pick?' The answer is: rank customers by predicted churn probability and take the top 500.

This is equivalent to asking: 'what threshold captures exactly 500 customers?' and finding that threshold empirically from the predicted probability distribution.

Option A is wrong: lowering the threshold to 0.1 might produce 5,000 flagged customers, far exceeding the 500-person capacity. Recall maximisation without a capacity constraint is a different problem.

Option B is wrong: 0.5 is not 'mathematically correct' in any universal sense. It is a common default that often does not match business constraints. Here it produces only 500 × 0.40/0.55 ≈ 360 actual churners out of 500 contacted, which may be improvable.

Option D is wrong: raising the threshold reduces the number of customers flagged, potentially leaving the retention team with fewer than 500 to contact and wasting capacity.
hints: The capacity constraint is '500 customers per week', not 'customers above probability 0.5'. These are different problems. Which framing directly answers the question 'who should we contact this week'?

Rank-based selection (top-500) and threshold-based selection (probability > x) are equivalent when the threshold is chosen to produce exactly 500 customers. Which is more directly actionable given the constraint?

title: Diagnosing Validation Curve Shapes
description: You plot validation curves for a decision tree varying max_depth from 1 to 20. At depth=1, train accuracy=0.65 and val accuracy=0.64. At depth=8, train accuracy=0.92 and val accuracy=0.87. At depth=15, train accuracy=0.99 and val accuracy=0.71. What do these three regions of the curve reveal, and what is the optimal depth?
options: Depth 1 is optimal — the gap is smallest, indicating the best generalization
Depth 15 is optimal — highest training accuracy means the model learned the most from the data
Depth 8 is optimal — it sits in the sweet spot where both train and val accuracy are high and the gap is reasonable; depth 1 is underfit and depth 15 is overfit
The validation curve is inconclusive; try a random forest instead
explanation: The three regions illustrate the full bias-variance spectrum. At depth=1, both train and val accuracy are low (≈0.64–0.65) — classic underfitting (high bias). The model is too simple to capture the data's signal. At depth=8, train accuracy is high (0.92) and val accuracy is still strong (0.87) — the model has learned meaningful patterns that generalize. At depth=15, training accuracy is near-perfect (0.99) but val accuracy has dropped to 0.71 — the model has memorized training noise (high variance, overfitting). The sweet spot is depth=8, where the validation curve peaks before diverging from the training curve.
hints: Look at both the absolute level and the train/val gap at each depth.
High train accuracy + low val accuracy = overfitting. Low train accuracy = underfitting.

title: When to Use One-vs-Rest vs Softmax for Multiclass
description: You are building a 5-class classifier using logistic regression. Your dataset is linearly separable between some class pairs but not others. Should you use One-vs-Rest (OvR) or multinomial (softmax) logistic regression?
options: Always use OvR — it is simpler and always outperforms softmax on real data
Always use softmax — it optimizes a single joint loss and is always more accurate
Use softmax when the classes are mutually exclusive and the dataset is large enough; OvR when you want independent calibration per class or when one class is much harder to separate than others
OvR and softmax are mathematically equivalent for 5 classes; the choice doesn't matter
explanation: OvR trains one binary classifier per class (class k vs all others), fitting 5 independent models. Each can independently optimize its decision boundary without interference from other classes. This is useful when class separability varies or when you want per-class probability calibration. Multinomial (softmax) logistic regression fits a single model with shared parameters across all classes, jointly optimizing a cross-entropy loss. It produces coherent probability distributions (sum to 1) and typically performs better when classes are mutually exclusive and the joint structure is well-captured by a linear model. For most standard multiclass problems, softmax is preferred; OvR is preferred when you need independent models or have heavily asymmetric class difficulties.
hints: OvR trains 5 separate binary classifiers. Softmax trains one multi-output model.
What happens to probability calibration when you average 5 independent classifiers vs optimize a joint loss?

title: Feature Scaling: When It Matters and When It Doesn't
description: A data scientist scales all features before training. Their colleague argues this was unnecessary. They are testing: (A) logistic regression, (B) random forest, (C) k-nearest neighbors, (D) gradient boosting. For which models is feature scaling necessary for correctness or performance, and for which is it irrelevant?
options: Scaling is necessary for all four — unscaled features always degrade model performance
Scaling is necessary for A and C; irrelevant for B and D — tree-based models use rank-based splits that are invariant to monotonic transformations of feature values
Scaling is necessary for B and D; irrelevant for A and C — gradient methods are stable without scaling
Scaling is only necessary when features have units (e.g., meters vs kilometers)
explanation: Logistic regression (A) uses gradient descent on a weighted sum of features — if one feature has range [0, 1000] and another [0, 1], the gradient updates are dominated by the large-scale feature, slowing convergence and potentially finding a worse solution. K-nearest neighbors (C) computes distances in feature space — features with larger ranges dominate the distance metric, making them implicitly more important. Both require scaling. Random forest (B) and gradient boosting (D) use decision trees with rank-based splits: the split point for a feature depends only on the ordering of values, not their absolute scale. A monotonic transformation (including standardization) doesn't change which split is optimal, so scaling is irrelevant to tree performance.
hints: What operations does each algorithm perform on feature values — weighted sums, distances, or rank-based comparisons?
If you multiply a feature by 1000, does a decision tree split differently? Does a distance metric?

title: Predicting Behavior of Nested Cross-Validation
description: You implement nested cross-validation: outer 5-fold CV to estimate generalization error, inner 3-fold CV to select hyperparameters. For each outer fold, the inner CV selects a different optimal max_depth (values: 4, 4, 6, 4, 8 across 5 outer folds). The outer fold test scores are [0.82, 0.84, 0.79, 0.83, 0.76]. What does the variance in selected hyperparameters reveal, and what is the reported generalization estimate?
options: The generalization estimate is 0.84 (best outer fold score); hyperparameter variance indicates the model is unstable
The generalization estimate is 0.808 (mean of outer fold scores); hyperparameter variance indicates the optimal depth is data-dependent and the model's performance is sensitive to the training subset
The generalization estimate is 0.79 (median outer fold score); hyperparameter variance should be minimized by using a fixed depth
Nested CV is invalid when hyperparameters vary across folds; use standard CV instead
explanation: The generalization estimate from nested CV is the mean of outer fold test scores: (0.82 + 0.84 + 0.79 + 0.83 + 0.76) / 5 = 0.808. This is an unbiased estimate because hyperparameter selection (inner CV) is performed entirely within each outer fold's training set — the outer test set is never used for model selection. The variance in selected hyperparameters (4, 4, 6, 4, 8) reveals that the optimal depth is sensitive to which subset of data is used for training — a sign of instability or that the performance landscape is relatively flat across depths 4–8. This is informative: in deployment you'd use the most commonly selected depth (4) or retrain on all data with inner CV to select the final hyperparameter.
hints: Nested CV separates model selection (inner) from model evaluation (outer). Which scores form the generalization estimate?
If different train subsets select different depths, what does that say about how critical the depth hyperparameter is?

title: Interpreting Confusion Matrix for Business Decisions
description:
A binary classifier for loan default prediction produces this confusion matrix on 10,000 test cases:

- True Negative (predicted no default, actual no default): 7,200
- False Positive (predicted default, actual no default): 800
- False Negative (predicted no default, actual default): 400
- True Positive (predicted default, actual default): 600

The bank loses $5,000 per false negative and spends $200 per false positive in review costs. What is the total cost of errors and which error type should the bank prioritize reducing?
options: Total cost: $2,160,000; prioritize reducing false negatives because each costs 25x more than a false positive
Total cost: $2,160,000; prioritize reducing false positives because there are twice as many of them
Total cost: $320,000; both error types are equally important
Total cost: $160,000; false negatives are already low enough relative to true positives
explanation: Total cost = (400 FN × $5,000) + (800 FP × $200) = $2,000,000 + $160,000 = $2,160,000. False negatives (approved loans that default) dominate the cost: 400 × $5,000 = $2,000,000, representing 93% of total errors cost. False positives (rejected good borrowers) cost only $160,000 total. The 25x cost ratio ($5,000 vs $200) means the bank should lower the classification threshold to catch more defaults — even at the cost of more false positives. A lower threshold increases recall (reduces FN) while increasing FP, but the economics strongly favor this tradeoff. This is a classic asymmetric cost problem that pure accuracy metrics obscure.
hints: Cost of errors = (FN count × FN cost) + (FP count × FP cost). Calculate each separately.
If one error type costs 25x more, should you be willing to accept more of the cheaper error to reduce the expensive one?

title: Why Accuracy Fails for Imbalanced Datasets
description: A dataset has 950 negative samples and 50 positive samples (5% positive rate). A naive classifier that predicts 'negative' for every sample achieves 95% accuracy. What metric and threshold would reveal this classifier is useless?
options: Use F1 score — a naive all-negative classifier gets F1 = 0.0 because precision and recall on the positive class are both zero
Use AUC-ROC — a naive classifier achieves AUC = 0.5, which correctly signals random performance
Use balanced accuracy — it averages recall across both classes, giving (1.0 + 0.0) / 2 = 0.5 for the naive classifier
All three metrics above correctly expose the naive classifier; the choice depends on what is more communicable to stakeholders
explanation: All three metrics expose the naive classifier, each in a different way. F1 score on the positive class = 0.0 because recall (TP / (TP + FN)) = 0/50 = 0. AUC-ROC for a classifier that never predicts positive has a random-chance ROC curve, giving AUC = 0.5. Balanced accuracy averages per-class recall: (recall_negative + recall_positive) / 2 = (950/950 + 0/50) / 2 = 0.5. The best choice depends on context: F1 is most intuitive for practitioners; AUC-ROC is threshold-agnostic and useful for comparing models; balanced accuracy is easy to explain to non-technical stakeholders. All three are vastly better than raw accuracy for imbalanced problems.
hints: What is precision, recall, and F1 for a classifier that predicts the majority class every time?
AUC-ROC represents the probability that a random positive outranks a random negative — what is that for a constant predictor?

title: Selecting the Right Imputation Strategy by Mechanism
description:
You are analyzing missingness in three features of a healthcare dataset:
- `blood_pressure`: missing for 8% of patients, no correlation with demographics or other features
- `income`: missing for 31% of patients, strongly correlated with education level
- `mental_health_score`: missing for 19% of patients, and inspection reveals patients with worse scores are less likely to complete the survey

Match each feature to the correct missingness mechanism (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and the appropriate imputation strategy.
options: blood_pressure=MCAR (mean imputation), income=MAR (multiple imputation), mental_health_score=MNAR (no imputation possible)

blood_pressure=MCAR (simple imputation or complete case analysis is unbiased), income=MAR (multiple imputation using education as auxiliary), mental_health_score=MNAR (missingness indicator + pattern mixture model or sensitivity analysis)
All three are MAR because the missingness can be explained by observed data
blood_pressure=MNAR, income=MCAR, mental_health_score=MAR — the labels don't affect the imputation choice
explanation: MCAR (Missing Completely At Random): blood_pressure missingness is unrelated to any observed or unobserved variable — complete case analysis or simple imputation is unbiased. MAR (Missing At Random): income missingness is explained by education (an observed variable) — multiple imputation that conditions on education correctly recovers the distribution. MNAR (Missing Not At Random): mental_health_score missingness depends on the score itself (sicker patients skip) — this is the hardest case. Standard imputation is biased because the observed scores are systematically better than the true distribution. Approaches: include a missingness indicator as a feature, use pattern mixture models, or conduct sensitivity analysis to bound the inference.
hints: MCAR: missingness is independent of everything. MAR: missingness depends on observed data. MNAR: missingness depends on the missing value itself.
For which mechanism is complete case analysis (dropping missing rows) unbiased?

title: Gradient Descent Convergence: Batch vs Mini-Batch vs SGD
description: You are training a neural network on 1 million samples. You compare three optimizers: (A) full batch gradient descent, (B) mini-batch SGD with batch size 256, (C) stochastic gradient descent with batch size 1. Rank them by: convergence stability, memory usage, and final model quality.
options: A > B > C on all three dimensions — more data per gradient update is always better
A: stable but memory-prohibitive; B: moderate stability + practical memory usage + best final quality in practice; C: noisy convergence, minimal memory, often escapes local minima better than A
C > B > A on final quality because noisy gradients always regularize better
A and C are equivalent on memory since both use the same model parameters
explanation: Full batch (A): exact gradient with no noise → stable but slow convergence per epoch, requires fitting all 1M samples in memory (often infeasible), and can converge to sharp minima that generalize poorly. Mini-batch (B): noisy but consistent gradient → practical memory usage (only 256 samples per step), GPU-parallelizable, noisy enough to escape local minima but stable enough to converge reliably. Empirically achieves the best generalization. SGD with batch=1 (C): maximum noise → nearly always escapes local minima but convergence is slow and erratic, memory is minimal. Mini-batch is the dominant choice in practice because it balances all three dimensions. The noise from mini-batches acts as implicit regularization, often yielding flatter minima that generalize better than full-batch sharp minima.
hints: Memory usage scales with batch size. Gradient noise scales inversely with batch size.
Why might noisy gradient estimates produce models that generalize better than exact gradients?

title: Random Forest: When Adding More Trees Stops Helping
description: You train random forests with 10, 50, 100, 500, and 1000 trees. Validation accuracy stabilizes around 500 trees: 10→0.74, 50→0.81, 100→0.84, 500→0.86, 1000→0.86. Training time grows linearly with tree count. What does this plateauing behavior reveal about random forest variance reduction, and what is the optimal tree count?
options: Add more trees indefinitely — accuracy will keep improving given enough computation

The plateau reveals that variance reduction from averaging saturates; once the ensemble is diverse enough, adding more trees doesn't reduce error further — 500 trees is optimal given the compute/accuracy tradeoff
The plateau means the model is overfitting; reduce tree count to 100
The plateau means the data is too easy; use a more complex algorithm
explanation: Random forest reduces variance by averaging many independent trees. Early trees contribute the most: going from 10 to 50 trees adds 7 points of accuracy, 50 to 100 adds 3 more. The marginal gain diminishes because variance reduction is bounded — it can't fall below the irreducible error. Beyond 500 trees, the ensemble has enough diversity that additional trees add negligible information. Importantly, random forests do not overfit with more trees (unlike boosting) — accuracy on held-out data plateaus rather than declining. The practical optimum is 500 trees here: maximum accuracy at half the compute cost of 1000 trees. Selecting the elbow in the accuracy-vs-trees curve is standard practice.
hints: Each additional tree contributes less variance reduction than the last. What does this imply about when to stop?
Unlike boosting, does adding more trees to a random forest ever hurt generalization?

title: PCA Variance Explained and Dimensionality Selection
description: You apply PCA to a 200-feature dataset. The explained variance ratios for the first 10 components are: [0.31, 0.18, 0.12, 0.08, 0.06, 0.04, 0.03, 0.02, 0.02, 0.01]. Cumulative: [0.31, 0.49, 0.61, 0.69, 0.75, 0.79, 0.82, 0.84, 0.86, 0.87]. You need to select the number of components for a downstream classifier. Which approach is most principled?
options: Use 3 components — the cumulative explained variance reaches 61%, which is sufficient
Use all 200 components — discarding any variance loses information
Select the number of components that explains 90–95% of variance, or use cross-validation on the downstream task to find the optimal number that maximizes classifier performance
Select exactly 10 components — this is the standard for PCA
explanation: The 90–95% explained variance heuristic is a practical starting point: it ensures you retain most of the signal while achieving meaningful dimensionality reduction. Based on the cumulative EVR above, reaching 90% would require around 12–15 components (from the pattern of the first 10). However, explained variance doesn't directly optimize the downstream task — components with low explained variance might carry class-discriminative signal that matters for classification. The most principled approach is cross-validation: treat n_components as a hyperparameter and evaluate classifier performance for each candidate value. This directly optimizes what you care about (classification accuracy) rather than a proxy (explained variance).
hints: Explained variance measures information retained. Does more explained variance always mean better classification?
The first few components capture the most variance. After a certain point, additional components add diminishing information.

title: Model Selection: When Simpler Beats Complex
description: For a tabular customer satisfaction prediction task (5,000 samples, 25 features), you compare: logistic regression (AUC=0.78), gradient boosting (AUC=0.82), and a 3-layer neural network (AUC=0.80). The product team needs to explain individual predictions to customers. Gradient boosting is the highest performer but requires SHAP post-hoc explanations. What factors should determine the final model choice?
options: Always choose the highest AUC model — gradient boosting at 0.82
Always choose logistic regression — it is inherently interpretable and regulators prefer it

Choose based on the gap significance, explanation requirements, and operational constraints: a 0.04 AUC gap may not justify the interpretability cost for a 5,000-sample dataset with explanation requirements — logistic regression or a shallow tree may be preferable
Choose the neural network — it balances accuracy and can be explained with LIME
explanation: Model selection requires balancing multiple dimensions. The AUC gap (0.78 vs 0.82) is 4 points — meaningful but context-dependent. With only 5,000 samples, gradient boosting's advantage may not be statistically robust. The explanation requirement is critical: if customers need to understand why their satisfaction score is what it is, SHAP post-hoc explanations add operational complexity and may not satisfy regulators or customers who expect a simple reason. Logistic regression with interaction features might close most of the gap while providing inherent, auditable explanations per customer. The decision framework: (1) Is the accuracy gap clinically/business significant? (2) Does the explanation method satisfy the use case? (3) What are the maintenance/operational costs? Simpler is often better when explanations are first-class requirements.
hints: A 0.04 AUC difference at 5,000 samples — is that statistically robust or within confidence interval noise?
Post-hoc explanations (SHAP) are approximations. Inherent explanations (logistic regression) are exact. When does that distinction matter?

title: Debugging a Leaking Validation Pipeline
description: A pipeline preprocesses features using StandardScaler fit on the full dataset, then splits into train/val. The validation AUC is 0.91. After refactoring to fit StandardScaler only on training data: validation AUC drops to 0.84. The engineer claims the original pipeline was correct because 'StandardScaler doesn't use labels'. What is the bug and why is the engineer's reasoning wrong?
options: The engineer is correct — StandardScaler is unsupervised and doesn't leak label information, so both pipelines are valid

The bug is that StandardScaler fitted on all data uses validation set statistics (mean, std) to transform training features, giving the model implicit access to validation set distribution — the 0.07 AUC gap measures this leakage
The bug is that StandardScaler should not be used for this problem; use MinMaxScaler instead
The drop from 0.91 to 0.84 is within normal variance; no bug exists
explanation: The engineer's reasoning is subtly wrong. StandardScaler doesn't use labels — but it does use the *data distribution* of the validation set when fitted on all data. The scaler computes mean and standard deviation from both train and validation samples. When training features are scaled using statistics that include validation data, the training set has implicitly 'seen' the validation distribution. At evaluation time, features appear consistent with validation distribution in a way they wouldn't if the scaler had only seen training data. This is preprocessing leakage — the same category as fitting PCA on all data. The fix is always: fit any preprocessing transform on training data only, then apply (transform) to both train and validation.
hints: Unsupervised doesn't mean 'uses no information from validation'. What information does StandardScaler use from the data?
If validation mean and std influence the scaler, does the training set see any validation distribution information?
